questions.question_text: Sum of the squares of the order and degree (if defined) of a differential equation $2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2}=\sqrt{y^{''}-3}$ is
questions.question_html: Sum of the squares of the order and degree (if defined) of a differential equation $2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2}=\sqrt{y^{''}-3}$ is
questions.explanation_text: The given differential equation is $2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2}=\sqrt{y^{''}-3}$ The highest order derivative present is $y^{''}$ , so the order of the differential equation is $2$ To find the degree, the equation must be written as a polynomial in derivatives. Since $y^{''}$ is inside a square root, we first remove the radical by squaring both sides: $(2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2})^{2}=y^{''}-3$ Expanding, $4(y^{'})^{2}+4y^{'}(y^{''})^{2}+(y^{''})^{4}=y^{''}-3$ Bring all terms to one side: $(y^{''})^{4}+4y^{'}(y^{''})^{2}+4(y^{'})^{2}-y^{''}+3=0$ Now it is a polynomial in derivatives. The highest order derivative is $y^{''}$ , and its highest power is $4$ . So, $\text{order}=2$ $\text{degree}=4$ Sum of the squares: $2^{2}+4^{2}=4+16=20$ So the correct option is $20$ Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is

$2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2}=\sqrt{y^{''}-3}$

The highest order derivative present is $y^{''}$ , so the order of the differential equation is

$2$

To find the degree, the equation must be written as a polynomial in derivatives. Since $y^{''}$ is inside a square root, we first remove the radical by squaring both sides:

$(2y^{'}+(y^{''})^{2})^{2}=y^{''}-3$

Expanding,

$4(y^{'})^{2}+4y^{'}(y^{''})^{2}+(y^{''})^{4}=y^{''}-3$

Bring all terms to one side:

$(y^{''})^{4}+4y^{'}(y^{''})^{2}+4(y^{'})^{2}-y^{''}+3=0$

Now it is a polynomial in derivatives. The highest order derivative is $y^{''}$ , and its highest power is $4$ .

So,

$\text{order}=2$

$\text{degree}=4$

Sum of the squares:

$2^{2}+4^{2}=4+16=20$

So the correct option is

$20$

Option B.

questions.question_text: $\int xf(x)dx+\frac{f(x)}{2}=0$ , then $f(x)$ is equal to
questions.question_html: $\int xf(x)dx+\frac{f(x)}{2}=0$ , then $f(x)$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\int xf(x)dx+\frac{f(x)}{2}=0$ Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ . The derivative of $\int xf(x)dx$ is $xf(x)$ , and the derivative of $\frac{f(x)}{2}$ is $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{2}$ . So, $xf(x)+\frac{f^{'}(x)}{2}=0$ Multiply by $2$ : $2xf(x)+f^{'}(x)=0$ So, $f^{'}(x)=-2xf(x)$ Now separate the variables: $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}=-2x$ This means $\frac{1}{f(x)}\frac{df}{dx}=-2x$ Integrate both sides: $\int \frac{1}{f}df=\int -2xdx$ $ln|f|=-x^{2}+C$ So, $f(x)=Ce^{-x^{2}}$ Among the given options, the matching function is $e^{-x^{2}}$ So the correct option is Option C .
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\int xf(x)dx+\frac{f(x)}{2}=0$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ .

The derivative of $\int xf(x)dx$ is $xf(x)$ , and the derivative of $\frac{f(x)}{2}$ is $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{2}$ .

So,

$xf(x)+\frac{f^{'}(x)}{2}=0$

Multiply by $2$ :

$2xf(x)+f^{'}(x)=0$

So,

$f^{'}(x)=-2xf(x)$

Now separate the variables:

$\frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}=-2x$

This means

$\frac{1}{f(x)}\frac{df}{dx}=-2x$

Integrate both sides:

$\int \frac{1}{f}df=\int -2xdx$

$ln|f|=-x^{2}+C$

So,

$f(x)=Ce^{-x^{2}}$

Among the given options, the matching function is

$e^{-x^{2}}$

So the correct option is Option C.

questions.question_text: Integrating factor of the differential equation $(1+x^{2})\frac{dy}{dx}+xy=1$ is
questions.question_html: Integrating factor of the differential equation $(1+x^{2})\frac{dy}{dx}+xy=1$ is
questions.explanation_text: The given differential equation is $(1+x^{2})\frac{dy}{dx}+xy=1$ First write it in the standard linear form $\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ Divide the whole equation by $1+x^{2}$ : $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}y=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$ So, $P=\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}$ For a linear differential equation, the integrating factor is $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int Pdx}$ Thus, $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{x}{1+x^{2}}dx}$ Now, $\int \frac{x}{1+x^{2}}dx=\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})$ So, $\text{I.F.}=e^{\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})}$ Using $e^{loga}=a$ , $\text{I.F.}=(1+x^{2})^{1/2}$ Hence, $\text{I.F.}=\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ So the correct option is $\text{Option D}\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is

$(1+x^{2})\frac{dy}{dx}+xy=1$

First write it in the standard linear form

$\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$

Divide the whole equation by $1+x^{2}$ :

$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}y=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$

So,

$P=\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}$

For a linear differential equation, the integrating factor is

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int Pdx}$

Thus,

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{x}{1+x^{2}}dx}$

Now,

$\int \frac{x}{1+x^{2}}dx=\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})$

So,

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\frac{1}{2}log(1+x^{2})}$

Using $e^{loga}=a$ ,

$\text{I.F.}=(1+x^{2})^{1/2}$

Hence,

$\text{I.F.}=\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$

So the correct option is

$\text{Option D}\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$

Now, $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{ℎ}{k}=-\frac{y}{x}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{y}=-\frac{dx}{x} \\ & \text{On integrating both sides, we get} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \int \frac{dy}{dy}=-\int \frac{dx}{x} \\ \Rightarrow & lny=-lnx+lnC \\ \Rightarrow & lny=ln\frac{C}{x} \\ \Rightarrow & y=\frac{C}{x} \\ \therefore & xy=C \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}+(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{2}=\sqrt[3]{}$ On cubic both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} & [1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}+(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{2}]^{3}=(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+1) \\ \Rightarrow & [1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}]^{3}+(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{6}+3[1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}] \cdot \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \\ & [1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}+(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{2}]=\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+1 \end{aligned}$ So, degree of the differential equation is 6 .
questions.explanation_html:

$1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}+(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{2}=\sqrt[3]{}$

questions.question_text: If a curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ and at any point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the product of the slope of its tangent and $x$ coordinate of the point is equal to the $y$ coordinate of the point, then the curve also passes through the point
questions.question_html: If a curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ and at any point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the product of the slope of its tangent and $x$ coordinate of the point is equal to the $y$ coordinate of the point, then the curve also passes through the point
questions.explanation_text: Let the equation of the curve by $y=f(x)$ and curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ , So, $f(1)=1$ Also, we know that at any point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the product of the slope of its tangent and $x$ co-ordinate of the point is equal to the $y$ co-ordinate of the point. $\begin{aligned} \frac{y}{x} & =\frac{dy}{dx} \\ xy^{'} & =y \end{aligned}$ $\frac{y^{'}}{y}=\frac{1}{x}$ On integrating both sides w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} ln|y| & =|In|x|+e^{c} \\ y & =kx,\text{where}k=e^{c} \end{aligned}$ Now, we can use the fact that the curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ to find the value of $k$ . $\Rightarrow l=k(l)k=1$ Therefore, the equation of the curve is $y=x$ Substituting the value of $x$ and $y$ from the given option, we find that the curve passes through the point $(2,2)$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the equation of the curve by $y=f(x)$ and curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ , So, $f(1)=1$ Also, we know that at any point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the product of the slope of its tangent and $x$ co-ordinate of the point is equal to the $y$ co-ordinate of the point.

$\begin{aligned} \frac{y}{x} & =\frac{dy}{dx} \\ xy^{'} & =y \end{aligned}$

$\frac{y^{'}}{y}=\frac{1}{x}$

On integrating both sides w.r.t. $x$ , we get

$\begin{aligned} ln|y| & =|In|x|+e^{c} \\ y & =kx,\text{where}k=e^{c} \end{aligned}$

Now, we can use the fact that the curve passes through the point $(1,1)$ to find the value of $k$ .

$\Rightarrow l=k(l)k=1$

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $y=x$

Substituting the value of $x$ and $y$ from the given option, we find that the curve passes through the point $(2,2)$

questions.explanation_text: We have, $\begin{aligned} & x^{2}dy-2xydx=x^{4}cosxdx \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{2}{x}y=x^{2}cosx \end{aligned}$ Comparing with $\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ Where $P=-\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q=x^{2}cosx$ . $\therefore \text{IF}=e^{\int \frac{-2}{x}dx}=e^{-2logx}=e^{log(\frac{1}{x^{2}})}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ $\therefore$ The solution of the given differential $\begin{aligned} y \cdot IF & =\int (Q \times IF)dx+c \\ \Rightarrow & y \times \frac{1}{x^{2}}=\int (x^{2}cosx)(\frac{1}{x^{2}})dx+c \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{y}{x^{2}}=\int cosx+c \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{y}{x^{2}}=sinx+c \\ \Rightarrow & y=x^{2}sinx+cx^{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The order of the differential equation obtained by eliminating arbitrary constants in the family of curves $c_{1}y=(c_{2}+c_{3})e^{x+c_{4}}$ is
questions.explanation_text: We have, $c_{1}y=(c_{2}+c_{3})e^{x+c_{4}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow y=(\frac{c_{2}+c_{3}}{c_{1}})e^{c_{4}} \cdot e^{x} \\ & \Rightarrow y=ce^{x}\text{where}c=\frac{c_{2}+c_{3}}{c_{1}}e^{c_{4}} \end{aligned}$ Taking $log$ on both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} & logy=log(ce^{x}) \\ \Rightarrow & logy=logc+xloge \\ \Rightarrow & logy=logc+x \end{aligned}$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=y$ $\therefore$ order $=1$
questions.explanation_html:
We have, $c_{1}y=(c_{2}+c_{3})e^{x+c_{4}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow y=(\frac{c_{2}+c_{3}}{c_{1}})e^{c_{4}} \cdot e^{x} \\ & \Rightarrow y=ce^{x}\text{where}c=\frac{c_{2}+c_{3}}{c_{1}}e^{c_{4}} \end{aligned}$

Taking $log$ on both sides, we get

$\begin{aligned} & logy=log(ce^{x}) \\ \Rightarrow & logy=logc+xloge \\ \Rightarrow & logy=logc+x \end{aligned}$

On differentiating w.r.t. $x$ , we get

$\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=y$

$\therefore$ order $=1$

questions.question_html: The order of the differential equation $y=C_{1}e^{C_{2}+x}+C_{3}e^{C_{4}+x}$ is
questions.explanation_text: We have, $y=C_{1}e^{C_{2}+x}+C_{3}e^{C_{4}+x}$ $\Rightarrow y=C_{1}e^{C_{2}}e^{x}+C_{3}e^{C_{4}}e^{x} \Rightarrow y=A \cdot e^{x}+B \cdot e^{x}$ (Here, $A=C_{1}e^{C_{2}},B=C_{3}e^{C_{4}}$ ) $\Rightarrow y=(A+B)e^{x}=Ce^{x}\text{(Here,}A+B=C)$ Here, number of arbitrary constant is one so, order of the differential equation is one.
questions.explanation_html:
We have, $y=C_{1}e^{C_{2}+x}+C_{3}e^{C_{4}+x}$

$\Rightarrow y=C_{1}e^{C_{2}}e^{x}+C_{3}e^{C_{4}}e^{x} \Rightarrow y=A \cdot e^{x}+B \cdot e^{x}$

(Here, $A=C_{1}e^{C_{2}},B=C_{3}e^{C_{4}}$ )

$\Rightarrow y=(A+B)e^{x}=Ce^{x}\text{(Here,}A+B=C)$

Here, number of arbitrary constant is one so, order of the differential equation is one.

questions.question_html: The degree and the order of the differential equation $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{}$ respectively are
questions.explanation_text: To find the degree and the order of the differential equation, consider the given equation: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{}$ To simplify the equation, cube both sides: $(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}})^{3}=1+(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}$ Now, identify the order and degree of the equation. The order is determined by the highest derivative present, which in this case is $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ . Therefore, the order is 2. The degree is determined by the power of the highest derivative after the equation has been expressed in polynomial form (if possible). Since the highest power of $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ in this equation is 3, the degree is 3. Thus, the differential equation has a degree of 3 and an order of 2.

questions.question_html: The solution of the differential equation $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=3$ represents a family of
questions.explanation_text: To solve the differential equation $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=3$ , we start by rewriting it: $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=3$ Rearrange the terms to isolate the derivatives: $xdy=(y+3)dx$ Separate variables to integrate both sides: $\frac{dy}{y+3}=\frac{dx}{x}$ Now, integrate both sides: $\int \frac{dy}{y+3}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$ After integration, we have: $log(y+3)=logx+logc$ This can be rewritten as: $log(y+3)=log(cx)$ Exponentiating both sides, we find: $y+3=cx$ This equation, $y=cx-3$ , represents a family of straight lines.
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the differential equation $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=3$ , we start by rewriting it:

$x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=3$

Rearrange the terms to isolate the derivatives:

$xdy=(y+3)dx$

Separate variables to integrate both sides:

$\frac{dy}{y+3}=\frac{dx}{x}$

Now, integrate both sides:

$\int \frac{dy}{y+3}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$

After integration, we have:

$log(y+3)=logx+logc$

This can be rewritten as:

$log(y+3)=log(cx)$

Exponentiating both sides, we find:

$y+3=cx$

This equation, $y=cx-3$ , represents a family of straight lines.

questions.question_text: The integrating factor of $\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1+y}{x}$ is
questions.question_html: The integrating factor of $\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1+y}{x}$ is
questions.explanation_text: To solve for the integrating factor, we start with the differential equation: $\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1+y}{x}$ By manipulating the equation, it can be rewritten as: Subtract $\frac{y}{x}$ from both sides: $\frac{dy}{dx}+y-\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{x}$ Rearrange to: $\frac{dy}{dx}+(1-\frac{1}{x})y=\frac{1}{x}$ In this form, we identify: $P=1-\frac{1}{x}$ $Q=\frac{1}{x}$ Next, we find the integrating factor (I.F.), given by: $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int Pdx}$ Calculate the integral of $P$ : $\int Pdx=\int (1-\frac{1}{x})dx=\int 1dx-\int \frac{1}{x}dx=x-logx$ Substituting back into the expression for the integrating factor: $\text{I.F.}=e^{(x-logx)}=\frac{e^{x}}{e^{logx}}=\frac{e^{x}}{x}$ Thus, the integrating factor is $\frac{e^{x}}{x}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To solve for the integrating factor, we start with the differential equation:

$\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1+y}{x}$

By manipulating the equation, it can be rewritten as:

Subtract $\frac{y}{x}$ from both sides:

$\frac{dy}{dx}+y-\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{x}$

Rearrange to:

$\frac{dy}{dx}+(1-\frac{1}{x})y=\frac{1}{x}$

In this form, we identify:

$P=1-\frac{1}{x}$

$Q=\frac{1}{x}$

Next, we find the integrating factor (I.F.), given by:

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int Pdx}$

Calculate the integral of $P$ :

$\int Pdx=\int (1-\frac{1}{x})dx=\int 1dx-\int \frac{1}{x}dx=x-logx$

Substituting back into the expression for the integrating factor:

$\text{I.F.}=e^{(x-logx)}=\frac{e^{x}}{e^{logx}}=\frac{e^{x}}{x}$

Thus, the integrating factor is $\frac{e^{x}}{x}$ .

questions.question_html:
General solution of differential equations

$\frac{dy}{dx}+y=1(y \ne 1)$ is
questions.explanation_text: We have, $\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}+y=1 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{dy}{dx}=1-y \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{1}{1-y}dy=dx \end{aligned}$ On integrating both the sides, we have $\begin{aligned} & \int \frac{1}{1-y}dy=\int dx \\ & \Rightarrow -log|1-y|=x+C \\ & \Rightarrow log|\frac{1}{1-y}|=x+C \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have,

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}+y=1 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{dy}{dx}=1-y \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{1}{1-y}dy=dx \end{aligned}$

On integrating both the sides, we have

$\begin{aligned} & \int \frac{1}{1-y}dy=\int dx \\ & \Rightarrow -log|1-y|=x+C \\ & \Rightarrow log|\frac{1}{1-y}|=x+C \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html:
The integrating factor of the differential equation

$x \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^{2}$ is $(x \ne 0)$
questions.explanation_text: To solve the differential equation, we start with: $x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^{2}$ Rewriting it in standard linear form, we have: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2}{x}y=x$ This is a linear differential equation, and to solve it, we need to find the integrating factor. The integrating factor, $\mu(x)$ , is given by: $\mu(x)=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}$ Calculating the integral, we get: $\mu(x)=e^{2logx}$ Using the properties of logarithms and exponents: $e^{2logx}=e^{logx^{2}}=x^{2}$ Thus, the integrating factor is $x^{2}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the differential equation, we start with:

$x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^{2}$

Rewriting it in standard linear form, we have:

$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2}{x}y=x$

This is a linear differential equation, and to solve it, we need to find the integrating factor. The integrating factor, $\mu(x)$ , is given by:

$\mu(x)=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}$

Calculating the integral, we get:

$\mu(x)=e^{2logx}$

Using the properties of logarithms and exponents:

$e^{2logx}=e^{logx^{2}}=x^{2}$

Thus, the integrating factor is $x^{2}$ .
